Manchester at a glance

Manchester is the largest city in New Hampshire, on the Merrimack River, and shares the Hillsborough County seat with Nashua. Residents numbered 115,644 at the 2020 census, with 116,818 estimated for 2025. The city covers 34.93 square miles, 33.07 of them land. It lies 18 miles south of Concord, 18 miles north of Nashua and 51 miles north-northwest of Boston.

Healthcare, education, finance and technology anchor the local economy, and the old mill complexes now hold offices instead of looms. Manchester is a single school district and a single tax jurisdiction, so your neighborhood does not change your tax rate. What changes with the neighborhood is the likely buyer, the shape of the lot and how near you are to the mills, downtown or the highway.

Neighborhoods and mill-era housing

The 2010 Master Plan defines 25 neighborhoods. None has legal or political authority and only some have associations, but buyers and agents use the names, so they show up in listings.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame and McGregorville, and Piscataquog (Granite Square)
  • East Side: North End, Janeville and Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Periphery: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

Textile mills built much of Manchester, and the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company's company town was founded on the eastern bank in 1838. Many houses near the old mills date from that boom, including multi-family buildings. An older multi-family building can bring deferred repairs and tenant questions into the same sale, so sort out leases and maintenance records before you talk price.

Tax rate and bill dates

Manchester's 2025 tax rate is $20.24 per $1,000, and the 2025 assessment ratio is 64.8%. The rate has four parts.

2025 tax rate components
Part of the rateRate per $1,000
Municipal10.04
County1.36
Local education7.33
State education1.51
Total20.24

The tax year runs April 1 to March 31, and bills go out twice. The first bill goes out in late May or early June, the second in mid to late November, and each is payable 30 days after it is mailed. The first bill uses half of the prior year's rate. The state sets the new rate in October or November, ahead of the second bill.

What happens when Manchester taxes are not paid

Manchester charges 8% a year on delinquent taxes under RSA 76:13, and unpaid balances can move to a lien. Before a lien is executed, certified mail delivers a notice of impending lien at least 30 days ahead, and after that interest accrues at 14% a year.

Two years of nonpayment after the lien lets the tax collector issue a tax deed to the city under RSA 80:76. Buying the property back after the deed means paying the back taxes, interest and costs plus a penalty equal to 10% of the equalized assessed value. The city also charges $10 per property for lien-release research and $2 per receipt.

Selling before a lien is executed avoids the 14% rate and the deed risk. Request a written payoff from the Tax Collector and pass it to whoever handles your closing.

Selling a rental house

The city requires every residential rental property to have a Certificate of Compliance under Chapter 150, the Housing Code, of its Code of Ordinances. An application is required for any new, vacant or previously owner-occupied residential rental that is to be rented or offered for rent.

If you own a rental with a valid certificate and sell it, a Transfer of Ownership form assigns the certificate to the new owner. The Building Department asks for the form with a $50 check payable to the City of Manchester and does not take these applications electronically. Housing inspections are by appointment only, at 603-624-6450.

Anyone buying to rent the house must sort out the certificate, so make sure yours is current before listing.

Flood zones and getting around

The Merrimack and Piscataquog rivers and Cohas Brook drain the city, and the rivers have flooded before. The state seller disclosure form includes a flood hazard zone question. Near the water? Look up your flood zone status before you answer it.

Interstates 93 and 293 meet near the Mall of New Hampshire. Manchester-Boston Regional Airport is in the city, the Manchester Transit Authority runs local buses, and Zip Line express routes reach Concord, Nashua and Salem. Easy highway and airport access is a real selling point for a house here.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Manchester houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Closing costs, disclosures and assessment appeals

RSA 78-B sets a real estate transfer tax of $.75 for each $100 of the price, owed by the buyer and by the seller. Granite Tax Connect is the filing route, and the settlement statement shows your share.

RSA 477:4-d makes a one to four family seller put certain facts in writing: private water and sewage systems, insulation, any federally designated flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank.

Think your assessment runs high? The city must receive your abatement application by March 1 after the final bill, and any appeal has a September 1 filing date. Collect recent comparable sales first.

How a cash sale works in Manchester

A cash sale lets a Manchester owner sell the house as-is, skipping repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal. You provide details, an offer follows, and the decision is yours.

A title search, tax proration, the transfer tax and the disclosure rules all still apply. Landlords should also confirm the rental certificate status, and anyone behind on taxes should get a payoff letter first. With those items ready, the closing can move as fast as you want it to. Before you accept, read the offer for the closing date, the price, who pays each closing cost and what happens to anything left in the house. You can decline any offer at no cost, so take the time to compare it with what a listing would likely bring.

Paperwork to gather before you list

Start with a written tax payoff from the Tax Collector, so you know whether anything is owed. If the house is a rental, confirm that the Certificate of Compliance is current and find the Transfer of Ownership form. Check the flood zone if the lot is near the Merrimack, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook. Landlords should also collect lease copies, rent records and any repair history for the building.

Those four items answer most of the questions a buyer, an inspector or a closing office will ask. Having them ready saves days, and it lets you compare a listing against a cash offer with real numbers in hand.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is Manchester's 2025 property tax rate?

The rate is $20.24 per $1,000 of assessed value: $10.04 municipal, $1.36 county, $7.33 local education and $1.51 state education. The 2025 assessment ratio is 64.8%.

When are Manchester tax bills due?

Two bills a year: one in late May or early June, one in mid to late November. Payment is due 30 days after each mailing.

Do I need a Certificate of Compliance to sell a rental in Manchester?

If the property is a rental with a valid certificate, the new owner needs a Transfer of Ownership form and a $50 fee to take it over. A new owner who rents a previously owner-occupied house needs a new application.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax?

The statute taxes both buyer and seller at $.75 per $100 of the price. Your contract and closing agent set out who pays which share.

How long can Manchester wait before taking a house for unpaid taxes?

The tax collector can execute a tax deed to the city two years after a lien, if taxes remain unpaid, after notice to owners and mortgagees.

Nashua at a glance

Nashua sits in southern New Hampshire, in southeastern Hillsborough County, and shares the county seat role with Manchester. Population is 92,435, and the city covers 31.73 square miles, of which 30.83 are land. The Massachusetts line is close, which shapes who shops and who buys here. Because New Hampshire has no sales tax, South Nashua's shopping district, anchored by Pheasant Lane Mall, pulls in shoppers from Massachusetts.

The city grew from textile mills into financial and professional services, high technology and defense. BAE Systems, Dell and Oracle have operations here, and two medical centers, Southern New Hampshire Medical Center and St. Joseph Hospital, serve the area.

Areas of the city

Nashua is usually described by district, and each has a different housing feel. These come up most when owners describe where a house sits:

  • Downtown, centered on Main Street, the oldest commercial district
  • The Tree Streets, a neighborhood near downtown reached by the Broad Street Parkway
  • The Millyard, the former mill district and the Nashua Manufacturing Company Historic District
  • French Hill, the northern area once called Nashville
  • The Amherst Street corridor (NH 101A) in the northwest
  • South Nashua, near the Massachusetts line

Living in or next to a historic district? Find out from the city what review exterior work needs before you count it as a pre-sale repair.

Tax rate and bill dates

Nashua's 2025 tax rate is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up 93 cents, or 5.83 percent, from the year before.

Recent Nashua tax rates
Tax yearRate per $1,000

Tax years run from April 1 to March 31. July 1 is the due date for the first bill, which uses half of last year's rate as an estimate. Once the state sets the new rate, the second bill follows, generally due by December 20. Abatement requests close March 1.

Taxes when you sell

Nashua prorates property taxes by the day from April 1 when a home is bought or sold. The closing agent calculates your portion for the settlement statement.

If you sold the property but still receive a bill, forward it to the current owner, or return it in the envelope with a note giving the sale date and the buyer's name. A new owner may see the old name for a while, since the Registry of Deeds has to send the transfer to the Assessor's Office. The city's property tax self-service portal shows what is owed, which makes it easy to confirm a zero balance before you pick a closing date.

How to challenge a Nashua assessment

Ask the Assessor's Office, at 603-589-3040, to review the data, then file a written abatement application by March 1. A request that misses March 1 cannot be acted on for the current tax year. You may still ask for a spring review, in which the Assessing Department may look at your value for the following tax year.

State law covers the next steps. The city answers by July 1, and if you want to go further, pick the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, never both, and file by September 1. The abatement does not stop collection, so pay the bill. A homeowner planning to sell should decide early whether the effort is worth it, since a buyer will care more about future bills than a past refund.

Transfer tax and seller disclosures

RSA 78-B gives New Hampshire a transfer tax of $.75 per $100 of the price, and the buyer and seller each owe it. Granite Tax Connect takes the filing.

Selling a one to four family home means a written statement under RSA 477:4-d covering private water and sewage systems, insulation, any federally designated flood hazard zone and any underground heating oil tank. Ask the title company what other charges will appear at closing, such as a mortgage payoff or any unpaid tax.

Winter, water and the buyer's inspection

Nashua has cold winters and wet springs, so a buyer's inspector will usually look at:

  • Roof condition after snow and ice
  • Basement moisture and lot drainage
  • Heating equipment and fuel storage
  • Insulation, which the state disclosure form asks about

Fixing small items before listing can help a financed sale hold together. Skipping that work is possible: a buyer paying cash as-is takes most of the list off the table.

Getting around Nashua

The Everett Turnpike is the main highway, and U.S. 3 follows it from the Massachusetts border to Exit 7E. NH 101A (Amherst Street), NH 111 (Hollis Street), NH 111A and NH 130 (Broad Street) also serve the city. The Broad Street Parkway, completed in 2015, connects Exit 6 to downtown.

The Nashua Transit System operates nine bus routes, and Boston Express runs from the Nashua Transit Center, near Exit 8, to South Station and Logan Airport. Nashua Airport (Boire Field) handles general aviation only, so air travelers use Manchester-Boston Regional or Logan. Commuter rail to Boston is only a proposal, so do not count on it when you price a house.

How a cash sale works in Nashua

Selling for cash in Nashua works like this: describe the house, review the offer and accept or pass, with no repairs and no lender appraisal. Title search, tax proration and the state transfer tax still happen. Ask the buyer to put the closing date, the price and who pays each closing cost in writing, and read the offer slowly before you sign. A fair buyer will not rush you, and you can say no at any point before closing.

Plan on three things before closing: a current tax payoff or confirmation that nothing is owed, your mortgage payoff if you have one, and a decision about what stays in the house. Once those are settled, the closing date is yours to pick within the title company's schedule.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Paperwork to gather before you list

Before you talk to a buyer or an agent, collect your latest tax bill, a copy of your deed and any permits for finished spaces or additions. Look up your account on the city portal to confirm nothing is owed, and call the Assessor's Office if the property record shows a different size or condition than the house really has. If you plan to ask for a spring review, note the date so it does not slip past March 1.

Add a short list of known repairs, including the roof, the heating system and any damp spots in the basement. Buyers and inspectors will find them anyway, and a seller who names them first usually keeps more control of the price. Photos taken before the house is emptied can also help if a question comes up later about what condition it was in.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Nashua tax rate for 2025?

It is $16.83 per $1,000 of valuation, up from $15.90 in 2024.

When are Nashua property tax bills due?

July 1 is the first due date, on a bill estimated at half of last year's rate. The second bill comes after the state sets the rate and is generally due by December 20.

Are Nashua property taxes prorated when I sell?

Yes. The city prorates by the day starting April 1 when a home changes hands, and the closing agent shows your share.

What if I missed the March 1 abatement deadline in Nashua?

No action can be taken for that tax year. You may request a spring review, which may lead to a review of your value for the following year.

Is there a sales tax or transfer tax on a Nashua house sale?

Buyer and seller each owe a state transfer tax of $.75 per $100 of the price. New Hampshire has no general sales tax.

Selling in Concord?

Concord at a glance

New Hampshire's capital, Concord, is also the Merrimack County seat. Population is 44,597, and the city covers 67.19 square miles, so a Concord address can mean a downtown apartment, a village farmhouse or a lot on a back road. Manchester lies about 16 miles south and Boston 66 miles south.

Downtown includes the North End and South End neighborhoods, and four villages sit around it:

  • Penacook
  • Concord Heights
  • East Concord
  • West Concord

Most homes fall in the Concord School District. Penacook belongs to the Merrimack Valley School District and has a higher tax rate, as the next section shows. Interstates 89 and 93 join just south of the city limits, I-393 heads east toward the Seacoast, and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport lies 23 miles to the south. Many buyers here work for the state or the hospital, so commute and move-in timing often drive their offers.

Tax rate, ratio and assessing office

The tax year in Concord runs from April 1 through March 31. The 2025 equalization ratio is 60.4%, which means assessed values sit well below what homes sell for. Dividing a total assessed value by that ratio gives a rough market value.

2025 property tax rates by area
AreaRate per $1,000 of assessed valueSchool district
Concord (most of the city)$29.11Concord School District
Penacook$30.74Merrimack Valley School District

The last citywide update before 2026 took effect April 1, 2021. Concord then carried out a full revaluation for tax year 2026, with Vision Government Solutions doing the field and data work. Your new value may differ a lot from the old one, and the rate moves too, so do not multiply a new assessment by last year's rate to guess your bill. Late payments carry interest at 8%, prorated daily.

The assessing office is at 41 Green Street, phone 603-225-8550. Call there with questions about your property record card, square footage or the condition notes on your house.

How to contest your assessment

To dispute your value, send the city an abatement application no later than March 1 after the final tax bill is issued. Abatements can be granted for good cause, usually an assessment error or a disproportionate assessment. The municipality has until July 1 to grant or deny the request. Still unhappy with the decision? Take the case to either the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, never both, with a filing deadline of September 1.

The bill stays payable while the request is pending, so pay it in full as issued. If an abatement is granted, a refund with interest follows. Saying your taxes feel high will not win a case. Back it up with comparable sales or an appraisal.

  1. Get your property record card and look for mistakes in size, age or features.
  2. Gather recent sales of similar Concord homes.
  3. Talk with the assessing office first.
  4. File the abatement application by March 1.
  5. Wait for the written answer, due by July 1.
  6. Appeal by September 1 if you still disagree.

What a Concord seller pays at closing

Under RSA 78-B, the state's real estate transfer tax is $.75 for every $100 of the sale price, and the law places it on the buyer and on the seller alike. Filing and payment go through the state's Granite Tax Connect portal. Your purchase agreement and the title company set out how the split is handled.

Expect these items on the settlement statement:

  • Transfer tax under RSA 78-B
  • Unpaid property tax for the current tax year
  • Any mortgage or lien payoff
  • Agent commission, if you list with an agent

Property tax is the other large line. The city's tax year begins April 1, so the current year's bill gets divided between you and the buyer; your closing agent will explain how. Deeds are recorded at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds, 163 N Main Street, Concord, phone (603) 228-0101. At your first meeting with the closing office, hand over a copy of your deed, the newest tax bill and a payoff request from your mortgage lender.

Disclosures every Concord seller owes

A seller of a one to four family home in New Hampshire has to supply a written disclosure before or while an offer is being prepared. RSA 477:4-d covers the private water supply, the private sewage system, insulation, flood hazard zone status and any underground heating oil tank.

If you do not know the answer on water, sewage or insulation, you have to say so in writing. The buyer signs to acknowledge receipt. A separate rule, RSA 477:4-c, applies before any purchase contract that includes a building. It asks for details such as the system's age, its last service date and the contractor who services it. Use the current version of the form and finish it before you accept an offer, so the contract does not stall.

Older homes and winter inspections

Many Concord houses are old, and some still have original wiring, plaster walls or a stone foundation. Concord winters are long, cold and snowy, and inspectors know it. Expect close attention to:

  • The roof and its ability to carry a heavy snow load
  • The heating system, its age and its fuel type
  • Pipes, insulation and any sign of water intrusion
  • The foundation and drainage after spring melt

Deferred work in these areas is a common reason a financed sale stalls. An as-is cash purchase means you do not repair any of it beforehand.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Concord houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

A Concord house can sell while taxes are unpaid. The balance, with interest, comes out of your proceeds at closing. Before signing a contract, get a current balance from the city. The title company also needs your latest bill so the next installment lands with the correct owner.

Check the timing as well. A closing just before or just after a billing date changes who owes what for the period, and a quick conversation with your closing agent settles it. If you also owe a mortgage or a lien, the payoff letters should be ordered early.

How a cash sale works for a Concord house

In a cash sale the buyer pays directly, with no bank appraisal or underwriting to wait on. Your timeline then rests on title work and your own calendar. You describe the property, get an offer and choose whether to take it. Nothing is owed if you decline.

The transfer tax, the property tax proration and the disclosure form still apply to a cash deal. What changes is that you skip repairs, showings and the financing contingency. This suits an older house with a worn roof or aging furnace, and it suits an estate that needs a closing date it can count on.

Whatever offer you consider, pin down the closing date, the split of closing costs and what happens to any belongings left in the house.

Frequently asked questions

Is Concord's property tax rate the same everywhere in the city?

No. The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000 for most of Concord and $30.74 for Penacook, which is served by the Merrimack Valley School District.

When is the deadline to appeal a Concord assessment?

Send the abatement application by March 1 after the final tax bill. Expect the city's answer by July 1, and file any further appeal by September 1.

Do both the buyer and the seller pay New Hampshire's transfer tax?

Yes, the statute imposes $.75 per $100 of the price on each of them. Your purchase agreement and title company set out who pays what at closing.

Does Concord have a revaluation affecting my sale?

Yes. Concord completed a full revaluation for tax year 2026, and the last citywide update before it took effect April 1, 2021. New values can change a buyer's tax estimate, so check your own notice.

Can I sell a Concord house with a private well or septic system?

Yes, though RSA 477:4-d requires you to hand the buyer the written water and sewage disclosure. Where you do not know an answer, write that down instead of leaving it blank.

Selling in Dover?

Dover at a glance

With 34,623 residents, Dover ranks fifth among New Hampshire cities and is the most populous city on the Seacoast. It is also the Strafford County seat. The Piscataqua River forms its eastern edge and the state line with Maine. The city covers 29.04 square miles, of which 26.73 are land, and most addresses sit in the Dover School District, which has about 4,000 pupils.

Dover claims the oldest permanent settlement in New Hampshire, begun in 1623 at Dover Point, and it became a city in 1855. Textile mills along Cochecho Falls built the downtown, and that left a stock of older homes close to the center. Homes from that era commonly have original wiring, aging plumbing or additions built without permits, which are exactly what inspectors flag.

The old mill complex has found new uses. Cocheco Falls Millworks now holds technology and government services companies, and the Children's Museum of New Hampshire occupies a former mill. Wentworth-Douglass Hospital is based in the city.

Getting in and out of Dover

Commuting access is one of the first things a Dover buyer asks about. The routes are NH 4, 9, 16 (the Spaulding Turnpike), 108 and 155, plus U.S. Route 4. Transit is broader than in many New Hampshire cities of this size:

  • Amtrak's Downeaster stops at the Dover Transportation Center, with service to Portland, Maine, and Boston North Station
  • C&J Bus Lines runs intercity service to Boston South Station, Logan Airport and the New York Port Authority
  • COAST operates a publicly funded bus network in New Hampshire and Maine
  • Wildcat Transit serves Durham, free for UNH students and $1.50 for the public

A house within reach of the train or the Spaulding Turnpike draws a different pool of buyers than one that is not, so mention the commute options when you describe your property.

Property tax rate and due dates

For 2025 the state Department of Revenue Administration certified Dover's rate at $19.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, built from four pieces.

Tax year 2025 rate components
Part of the rateRate per $1,000
City6.91
County1.83
State school1.16
City school9.78
Total19.68

Two bills arrive each year. Half is due December 1 and the other half June 1, and anything late collects interest at 12% a year. Exact dates can shift because the state sets the rate, so call the City Clerk and Tax Collector at 603-516-6018 before you rely on a date.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Dover house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Your assessment and how to appeal it

Dover did not run its annual citywide revaluation for tax year 2025. The assessment office judged that current values still met assessing standards, and skipping the update made for a cleaner move to a new computer-assisted mass appraisal system. The city mailed value change notices to 993 properties instead. The assessor estimated a 5% market increase for the year, and leaving values alone kept an equalization ratio of 89% to 90%. By state law, values reflect conditions on April 1, the first day of the tax year.

Believe your value is off? Submit an abatement application to the Tax Assessment Office by the March 1 that follows the tax year. Payment is still expected while you wait, so keep up with the bill. Should the city say no, or stay silent past July 1, you have until September 1 to go to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, but only one of them. The assessment office is at 603-516-6014.

If Dover taxes go unpaid

Unpaid Dover taxes can end in a lien and, eventually, a deed to the city. Certified notices go out in July, and liens are recorded at the Registry of Deeds in August, with interest at 18% a year on the lien amount from the lien date.

A lien can be redeemed within two years by paying everything owed plus interest and fees. A property with an unredeemed lien can be deeded to the city at least two years and one day after the lien date. A sale is one way to clear a balance before a lien forms, and a cash buyer does not need a lender to review the arrears.

When you owe back taxes, phone the Tax Collector and request a written payoff with interest figured through a specific date. Give the letter to whoever runs your closing, and the balance comes out of what you receive.

Permits on older Dover houses

Dover Inspection Services handles building permits from 269 Mast Road, next to the public works complex, and applications go through the city's online permit portal. The office can be reached at 603-516-6038.

The state codes in effect when a permit is applied for stay in force for that work, and Dover may adopt stricter building and fire codes by ordinance. If a previous owner finished a basement or added a deck, check that a permit exists before you list. Missing paperwork tends to surface during a buyer's inspection and can slow a financed sale. A cash buyer will still ask about it, but the conversation is usually simpler.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Dover houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and seller disclosures

Under RSA 78-B, each side of the sale, buyer and seller, owes the state $.75 on every $100 of the price. The Granite Tax Connect portal handles filing, and the settlement statement lists your exact amount.

RSA 477:4-d also requires owners of one to four family homes to put in writing what they know about private water and sewage, insulation, flood hazard zone status and any buried heating oil tank. Complete the form early so the contract is not delayed.

How a cash sale works in Dover

You describe your Dover house, an offer comes back, and you decide; saying no costs nothing. With no lender appraisal involved, repair demands from a financed buyer never get a chance to delay closing.

Title search, tax proration, the transfer tax and the disclosure rules all remain. Before you agree to a closing date, get your tax payoff, locate your permits and decide what you want to leave in the house. That short list keeps the timeline tight and avoids surprises at the table.

Paperwork to gather before you sell

Collect a few items before you call anyone: your latest tax bill, any permits for finished basements or decks, and a rough list of repairs you already know about. The Tax Assessment Office can supply your property record, and Inspection Services can tell you whether a permit was ever closed out. Knowing those answers up front shortens every conversation that follows, whether you list with an agent or take a cash offer.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is Dover's property tax rate?

The 2025 rate is $19.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, made up of 6.91 city, 1.83 county, 1.16 state school and 9.78 city school.

When are Dover property taxes due?

The first half is due December 1 and the second half June 1. Call the City Clerk and Tax Collector at 603-516-6018 to confirm a date.

How do I appeal my Dover assessment?

Submit an abatement application to the Tax Assessment Office by March 1 after the bill. A denial, or no answer by July 1, opens a window until September 1 to appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court, not both.

Is there a transfer tax when I sell a house in Dover?

Yes. Each of the buyer and the seller owes $.75 per $100 of the price under RSA 78-B, filed through the Granite Tax Connect portal.

Does Dover have train service for commuters?

Yes. Amtrak's Downeaster stops at the Dover Transportation Center, with service to Portland, Maine, and Boston North Station.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Rochester?
We buy Rochester houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Rochester at a glance

Rochester is a city in Strafford County in southeastern New Hampshire. Population is 33,716, which makes it one of the larger cities in the state. It covers 45.4 square miles, of which 45.0 is land, so a Rochester address can mean anything from a downtown lot to a rural road with acreage.

Three villages sit inside the city limits, and each has its own feel when a buyer or an appraiser looks at a house:

  • East Rochester
  • Gonic
  • North Rochester

All three are part of the City of Rochester, so they share one assessing department and one tax collector. The Spaulding Turnpike, NH Route 16, is the main artery, running south toward Dover and Portsmouth and north toward Conway, and COAST runs local buses.

Tax rate and bill dates

Rochester's 2025 rate, set by the state Department of Revenue Administration, is $15.30 per $1,000 of assessed value. It was $14.85 in 2024 and $25.74 in 2023. The 2025 rate breaks down as follows, on a net assessed valuation of $5.185 billion.

2025 tax rate components
Part of the rateRate per $1,000
City$4.45
County$1.77
Local school$7.98
State school$1.10
Total$15.30

Rochester bills twice a year. The summer bill is mailed in June and the winter bill in December, and each gives you about a month before interest starts. Check your bill for the exact date.

The Tax Collector is at 150 Wakefield Street, Suite 271. You can pay in person, by mail, online (for an added fee), through bank bill pay or in the night drop box. A returned payment, including a returned eCheck, costs $25.

What the 2024 revaluation changed

Rochester completed a citywide revaluation effective April 1, 2024, and the tax rate fell 42.3 percent because values rose sharply. The prior full revaluation was in 2019, and the state requires one at least every five years. The revaluation added $2.3 billion to the city's net assessed valuation.

A higher value does not automatically produce a higher bill. Homes that had been assessed well below market moved up the most, while homes already near market value changed little and some owners paid less. Manufactured homes drew the most attention: the mayor said some mobile home values had doubled and sometimes almost tripled.

The city's median sales ratio compares assessments to actual sale prices. It was 97.4 percent for 2024 and 93.2 percent for 2025. A ratio below 100 percent means sale prices are running somewhat above assessed values. Before the revaluation the ratio had been 64.3 percent for 2022, so older assessed values said very little about what a house would fetch.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Rochester house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to contest your assessment

To seek an abatement, apply to the city. RSA 76:16 puts the deadline at March 1 after the tax notice date. Only a person aggrieved by the assessment can apply, and the owner must have complied with RSA 74.

The assessors must grant or deny the application in writing by July 1 after the notice date. If they do not respond, the law treats that as a denial. A written decision has to explain the appeal route. RSA 76:16-a gives you until September 1 to take a disagreement to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals. The filing fee is $65, and you may choose a small claims procedure unless the city asks for a full hearing. Rochester's Assessing Department answers questions at (603) 332-5109 and offers appointments online.

The steps in order:

  1. Study your assessment notice next to recent sales of similar homes.
  2. Ask the Assessing Department to review your record.
  3. File the abatement application by March 1.
  4. Wait for the written decision, due by July 1.
  5. If needed, appeal by September 1.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing property tax does not block a Rochester sale. Your closing attorney pays the unpaid amount out of the proceeds at the table. Call the Tax Collector at 150 Wakefield Street for a payoff figure, and ask for one that is dated for your closing day.

If you owe on a mortgage as well, request that payoff at the same time. Having both letters in hand early lets the closing attorney tell you what you will take home before you commit to a date.

Tenants and manufactured homes

Rochester has a wide mix of housing, including single-family homes, small multi-unit buildings, larger apartment buildings and a meaningful number of mobile and manufactured homes. The mix affects how a sale works.

Owners of two- to four-unit buildings often sell with tenants in place. If you are in that position, tell any buyer early what leases exist and when the rent is paid. A cash buyer can take an occupied property, but the lease terms and notice rules under New Hampshire law still apply. Owners of manufactured homes should confirm how the 2024 revaluation changed their assessment before they set a price.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Rochester houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and local codes

Buyer and seller each owe the state a real estate transfer tax of $0.75 per $100 of the price. Payment runs through the Granite Tax Connect portal, and the Department of Revenue Administration call center is at (603) 230-5920.

The city's Building and Licensing Services office, at the City Hall Annex, 33 Wakefield Street, enforces local codes. Call (603) 332-3508 with questions about open permits or unfinished work. The codes in force include:

  • International Building Code, 2021 edition
  • International Residential Code, 2021 edition
  • International Energy Conservation Code, 2018 edition
  • National Electrical Code, 2023 edition
  • International Property Maintenance Code, 2015 edition
  • Life Safety Code and State Fire Code, enforced by the Fire Department

Check for open permits and unfinished work before any sale, whether conventional or cash.

How a cash sale of a Rochester house works

A cash buyer needs no mortgage, which means your timeline follows title work and your own schedule rather than a bank's appraisal. Tell us about the property, and after a review we send a written offer. You may decline it and owe nothing.

Cash buyers purchase houses as-is, so repairs, old furnishings and deferred maintenance stay with the buyer. A New Hampshire title or closing attorney settles any mortgage and unpaid property tax from your proceeds at closing, then records the deed at the Strafford County registry of deeds.

A cash sale does not suit every owner. A house in good condition, with time to spare, may do better on the open market. If you inherited it, are behind on payments, have tenants or face costly repairs, speed and certainty may matter more.

Paperwork to gather before you sell

Bring your latest tax bill, a copy of the deed and your mortgage statement to the first conversation with a closing attorney. If the building has tenants, add the leases and rent dates. Ask Building and Licensing Services about open permits, and ask the Assessing Department whether your record card matches the house. Each item is a quick call, and together they keep the closing date from slipping.

What is the property tax rate in Rochester, NH?

The 2025 rate is $15.30 per $1,000 of assessed value: $4.45 city, $1.77 county, $7.98 local school and $1.10 state school. The state sets the 2026 rate in late fall.

When are Rochester property taxes due?

Rochester bills twice a year, with a summer bill mailed in June and a winter bill mailed in December. Each allows about a month before interest starts, so check your bill for the exact date.

Can I sell my Rochester house if I owe property tax?

Yes. Your closing attorney pays the unpaid tax out of the proceeds at closing. Call the Tax Collector at 150 Wakefield Street for a payoff figure.

What is the New Hampshire transfer tax on a house sale?

Both the buyer and the seller owe the state $0.75 per $100 of the price.

How do I appeal my Rochester assessment?

The city must receive your abatement application by March 1 after the tax notice. A denial can be taken to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals by September 1.
